newsitem.title: USA: Six-person jury chosen in secondhand-smoke trial.
newsitem.headline: Six-person jury chosen in secondhand-smoke trial.

text.p: Three smokers and three non-smokers were chosen Wednesday as the jury to decide in a $5 billion anti-tobacco trial whether or not secondhand-smoke caused the lung cancer and other tobacco-related diseases of 60,000 U.S. flight attendants who never used cigarettes.

The jury of four men and two women, all from Florida, will hear eight weeks or more of attorneys' arguments and testimony expected to be dominated by scientific and medical experts debating the disputed claim that secondhand smoke causes lung cancer, heart disease and other ailments.
Norma Broin et al vs. Philip Morris et al seeks $5 billion or more from U.S. tobacco companies and is the first secondhand-smoke claim to make it to trial in the United States.
Opening statements by plaintiff attorneys Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt of Miami are to begin Monday morning in Dade County Court.

After five weeks of painstaking individual questioning by lawyers to identify 119 potential jurors, the jury of six was chosen in just over two hours with opposing lawyers excercising just 18 juror challenges they did not have to explain. Each side could have barred as many as 27 people without giving a reason.
Dade County Circuit Judge Robert Kaye immediately swore in the jurors, who were not identified by name.
"For better or worse, you folks have been sworn in as jurors on this case," Kaye told the six.

The lawyers, including a dozen or so for the tobacco industry, also chose 10 alternates, who will fill in any vacancies among the six-member jury caused by illness or other reasons. Seven women and three men were selected as the alternates.
"We were looking for people with common sense and broad life experiences," plaintiff Susan Rosenblatt said. "And we got them."
A spokesman for Reynolds Tobacco, one of the defendants, said the research linking secondhand smoke with cancer and other diseases had many holes in it and would be challenged throughout the trial.

The flight attendants claim their ailments were caused by passengers' cigarette smoke aboard U.S. airlines before smoking was banned on them in 1988. The Reynolds spokesman said the incidence of lung cancer and other ailments among the flight attendants was no greater than that of other groups of non-smokers.
